Projecting Peak Velocity from Pitching Mechanics¶

Out of the provided pitchers in the 2025 FCL dataset, which pitcher do you believe will throw the hardest in five years? You may construct any model(s) or metric(s) to support your conclusion. Deliverables: Your response should include: ● a clear description of your methodology, including all data processing and/or modeling steps, ● any quantitative and/or qualitative tests that you used to validate your approach, and ● all of the code that you used in preparing your solution.

Data Loading¶

In [1]:
# Data Load
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Data file paths come from config.py (data lives in the data/ directory)
from config import VELO_AND_MECHANICS, FCL_MECHANICS_2025, METRIC_DESCRIPTIONS

# Metric Descriptions
metrics_df = pd.read_csv(METRIC_DESCRIPTIONS)

# Velocity and Mechanics
mech_df = pd.read_csv(VELO_AND_MECHANICS)

# FCL Mechanics 2025
fcl_df = pd.read_csv(FCL_MECHANICS_2025)

Dataset structure¶

Is this a single snapshot per pitcher, or a panel? Multiple pitches per pitcher across more than one season means the unit of observation is the pitch, and a pitcher's rows are repeated measures — which matters for how we aggregate and model later.

In [5]:
per = d.groupby('pitcher_id').size()
dt  = pd.to_datetime(d['date'], format='%m/%d/%y', errors='coerce')
hand = d['pitcher_handedness'].value_counts(dropna=False)

print(f'Pitchers:         {d["pitcher_id"].nunique()}')
print(f'Rows per pitcher: min={per.min()}, median={per.median():.0f}, max={per.max()}')
print(f'Date range:       {dt.min().date()} → {dt.max().date()} '
      f'({dt.dt.year.nunique()} seasons)')
print('Handedness:       ' + ', '.join(f'{k}={v}' for k, v in hand.items()))

Outlier / data-quality scan¶

Large gaps between the 1st/99th percentiles and the min/max flag likely tracking errors (e.g. back_hip_flexion_at_ball_release min of −260°, lead_leg_internal_rotation_velo_max min of −8773). Worth clipping or winsorizing before modeling.

In [8]:
outlier = pd.DataFrame({
    'min': d[mech_cols].min(),
    'p01': d[mech_cols].quantile(0.01),
    'p99': d[mech_cols].quantile(0.99),
    'max': d[mech_cols].max(),
}).round(1)

Pitcher-level aggregation¶

The unit of observation above is the pitch, with 3–414 rows per pitcher, so pitch-level correlations are dominated by high-volume arms and violate independence. Since the question ("hardest in five years") is about a pitcher, collapse to one row per pitcher.

Two steps:

  1. Winsorize each mechanics column to its [p01, p99] range so the tracking errors flagged in the outlier scan don't distort per-pitcher means.
  2. Aggregate — velocity gets several summaries (peak is what matters, but raw max is noisy, so p95 is the more robust peak); mechanics get the winsorized mean; identifiers and a date span are carried through.
In [9]:
# Mechanics feature columns (numeric, excluding ids / target / height,
# which is handled separately as a summary field).
feature_cols = [c for c in d.columns
                if c not in ('date', 'pitcher_id', 'pitcher_handedness',
                             'velocity', 'player_height')
                and pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(d[c])]

# 1. Winsorize mechanics to [p01, p99] (per column)
lo, hi = d[feature_cols].quantile(0.01), d[feature_cols].quantile(0.99)
dc = d.copy()
dc[feature_cols] = dc[feature_cols].clip(lower=lo, upper=hi, axis=1)

# 2. Aggregate to one row per pitcher
g  = dc.groupby('pitcher_id')
dt = pd.to_datetime(dc['date'], format='%m/%d/%y', errors='coerce')
span = dt.groupby(dc['pitcher_id']).agg(['min', 'max'])

summary = pd.DataFrame({
    'handedness': g['pitcher_handedness'].agg(lambda s: s.mode().iat[0]),
    'height':     g['player_height'].median(),
    'n_pitches':  g.size(),
    'velo_mean':  g['velocity'].mean(),
    'velo_p95':   g['velocity'].quantile(0.95),  # robust peak
    'velo_max':   g['velocity'].max(),
    'velo_std':   g['velocity'].std(),
    'hss_max':    g['hip_shoulder_separation_max'].max(),  # pitcher PEAK hip-shoulder sep (winsorized) – a capacity signal,
                                                            # distinct from the averaged value in the mechanics block
    'first_seen': span['min'].dt.date,
    'last_seen':  span['max'].dt.date,
    'day_span':   (span['max'] - span['min']).dt.days,
})

# mechanics: winsorized per-pitcher means
pitcher_df = summary.join(g[feature_cols].mean())

print(f'{pitcher_df.shape[0]} pitchers × {pitcher_df.shape[1]} columns')
n_thin = (pitcher_df['n_pitches'] < 10).sum()
print(f'{n_thin} pitchers have <10 pitches — noisy aggregates, '
      f'candidates for filtering or sample-size weighting later.')

pitcher_df.head()

Re-check correlations on the aggregated data¶

Correlations of the winsorized mechanics means against each pitcher's velo_p95. Comparing these to the pitch-level ranking above shows how much the repeated-measures structure was inflating things.

In [10]:
agg_corr = (pitcher_df[feature_cols + ['velo_p95']]
            .corr(numeric_only=True)['velo_p95']
            .drop('velo_p95').sort_values(key=abs, ascending=False))

Modeling: predicting velocity from mechanics¶

Three models on pitcher_df (one row per pitcher), target = velo_p95 (robust peak velocity):

  1. XGBoost – nonlinearity / interaction check, with SHAP.
  2. Bayesian LASSO – linear, Laplace priors on the coefficients.
  3. Regularized horseshoe – the Python equivalent of brms horseshoe() (Piironen & Vehtari 2017), built in PyMC.

Both Bayesian models use standardized predictors and a standardized target, so the priors live on a common scale. Predictors include the winsorized mechanics means, height, and the new hss_max.

Requires pymc, arviz, xgboost, shap. The two metrics below are not directly comparable: XGBoost is scored with repeated K-fold CV RMSE, while the Bayesian models are scored with PSIS-LOO (out-of-sample) plus an in-sample posterior-predictive RMSE. For a single common metric, refit the Bayesian models under the same K-fold splits (heavier – left as an extension).

In [11]:
model_features = feature_cols + ['height', 'hss_max']

md = pitcher_df.dropna(subset=model_features + ['velo_p95']).copy()
X_raw = md[model_features].to_numpy(dtype=float)
y     = md['velo_p95'].to_numpy(dtype=float)

# Standardize for the linear (Bayesian) models; trees use raw X.
X_mean, X_sd = X_raw.mean(0), X_raw.std(0)
X_std = (X_raw - X_mean) / X_sd
y_mean, y_sd = y.mean(), y.std()
y_std = (y - y_mean) / y_sd

n, p = X_raw.shape
print(f'{n} pitchers, {p} predictors  (target: velo_p95, '
      f'mean={y_mean:.1f} sd={y_sd:.2f} mph)')

2. Bayesian LASSO¶

Laplace (double-exponential) priors on the standardized coefficients, with a shared scale b that controls overall shrinkage.

In [ ]:
import pymc as pm
import pytensor.tensor as pt
import arviz as az

with pm.Model() as lasso_model:
    Xd        = pm.Data('Xd', X_std)
    b         = pm.HalfCauchy('b', beta=1.0)            # global Laplace scale
    beta      = pm.Laplace('beta', mu=0.0, b=b, shape=p)
    intercept = pm.Normal('intercept', 0.0, 1.0)
    sigma     = pm.HalfNormal('sigma', 1.0)
    mu        = intercept + pt.dot(Xd, beta)
    pm.Normal('y', mu=mu, sigma=sigma, observed=y_std)
    lasso_idata = pm.sample(1500, tune=1500, target_accept=0.95,
                            chains=4, random_seed=42,
                            idata_kwargs={'log_likelihood': True})

print('max R-hat:', max(float(v.max()) for v in az.rhat(lasso_idata).data_vars.values()),
      '| divergences:', int(lasso_idata.sample_stats['diverging'].sum()))

Model assumptions & diagnostics¶

The Bayesian LASSO is a Gaussian linear regression with Laplace (double-exponential) priors. Its conclusions are only trustworthy if the modeling assumptions hold and the MCMC sampler actually explored the posterior. The assumptions we are relying on:

  • Linearity & additivity — velo_p95 is a linear, additive function of the standardized mechanics; no interactions or curvature are modeled (the XGBoost/SHAP block is the nonlinearity check).
  • Independence of observations — one row per pitcher, since the pitch-level repeated-measures structure was collapsed in the aggregation step, so residuals should be independent.
  • Homoscedasticity — a single residual scale sigma for every pitcher; residual spread should not grow with the fitted value.
  • Gaussian errors — residuals around the regression line are approximately normal.
  • Standardized predictors & target — X and y are z-scored, so the shared Laplace scale b shrinks every coefficient comparably and the prior is scale-free.
  • Sparsity prior is appropriate — the Laplace prior assumes most mechanics have ~zero effect and a few matter; with 64 correlated predictors and 203 pitchers this regularization is what keeps the fit identifiable.

The next cells check, in order: (1) sampler convergence — R-hat, ESS, MCSE, divergences, BFMI; (2) mixing and posterior geometry — trace and energy plots; (3) the likelihood and residual assumptions — a posterior-predictive check plus residuals-vs-fitted (homoscedasticity) and a normal Q-Q plot (normality).

# --- Likelihood + residual assumption checks ---
from scipy import stats

# Posterior-predictive draws from the fitted LASSO model
with lasso_model:
    lasso_ppc = pm.sample_posterior_predictive(
        lasso_idata, random_seed=42, progressbar=False)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4))

# (1) Posterior predictive vs observed (standardized scale): does the
#     Gaussian likelihood reproduce the shape of the target?
az.plot_ppc(lasso_ppc, num_pp_samples=100, ax=ax[0])
ax[0].set_title('Posterior predictive vs observed (z-scored y)')

# Residuals from the posterior-mean regression line, back on the mph scale
post   = lasso_idata.posterior
b_m    = post['beta'].mean(('chain', 'draw')).values
i_m    = float(post['intercept'].mean(('chain', 'draw')).values)
fitted = (i_m + X_std @ b_m) * y_sd + y_mean
resid  = y - fitted

# (2) Homoscedasticity: residual spread should not trend with the fitted value
ax[1].scatter(fitted, resid, alpha=0.6, edgecolor='white')
ax[1].axhline(0, color='k', lw=0.8)
ax[1].set(xlabel='Fitted velo_p95 (mph)', ylabel='Residual (mph)',
          title='Residuals vs fitted (homoscedasticity)')

# (3) Normality of errors: points should track the 45° line
stats.probplot(resid, dist='norm', plot=ax[2])
ax[2].set_title('Normal Q-Q of residuals')

for a in ax[1:]:
    a.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f'Residuals: mean={resid.mean():.3f} mph, sd={resid.std():.3f} mph '
      f'(in-sample RMSE={np.sqrt((resid**2).mean()):.3f})')
print(f'Shapiro-Wilk normality p = {stats.shapiro(resid).pvalue:.3f} '
      f'(> 0.05 = no evidence against normal errors)')

3. Regularized horseshoe (brms horseshoe() equivalent)¶

Finnish horseshoe: global scale tau set from a prior guess p0 of the number of relevant predictors, half-Cauchy local scales, and a Student-t slab that caps the largest coefficients. Non-centered parameterization for sampling stability.

In [ ]:
p0 = 10                                    # prior guess: ~10 relevant predictors
tau0 = (p0 / (p - p0)) * (1.0 / np.sqrt(n))  # global-scale prior (y is standardized)
slab_scale, slab_df = 2.0, 4.0

with pm.Model() as hs_model:
    Xd  = pm.Data('Xd', X_std)
    tau = pm.HalfCauchy('tau', beta=tau0)                  # global shrinkage
    lam = pm.HalfCauchy('lam', beta=1.0, shape=p)          # local shrinkage
    c2  = pm.InverseGamma('c2', alpha=slab_df / 2,
                          beta=slab_df / 2 * slab_scale**2)  # slab
    lam_t = pt.sqrt(c2) * lam / pt.sqrt(c2 + tau**2 * lam**2)
    z     = pm.Normal('z', 0.0, 1.0, shape=p)              # non-centered
    beta  = pm.Deterministic('beta', z * tau * lam_t)
    intercept = pm.Normal('intercept', 0.0, 1.0)
    sigma     = pm.HalfNormal('sigma', 1.0)
    mu        = intercept + pt.dot(Xd, beta)
    pm.Normal('y', mu=mu, sigma=sigma, observed=y_std)
    hs_idata = pm.sample(1500, tune=1500, target_accept=0.99,
                         chains=4, random_seed=42,
                         idata_kwargs={'log_likelihood': True})

print('max R-hat:', max(float(v.max()) for v in az.rhat(hs_idata).data_vars.values()),
      '| divergences:', int(hs_idata.sample_stats['diverging'].sum()))

In [ ]:






def insample_rmse(idata):
    post = idata.posterior
    b_m  = post['beta'].mean(('chain', 'draw')).values
    i_m  = float(post['intercept'].mean(('chain', 'draw')).values)
    pred = (i_m + X_std @ b_m) * y_sd + y_mean   # back to mph
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean((pred - y) ** 2)))

# LOO comparison (Bayesian models only; apples-to-apples)
compare = az.compare({'horseshoe': hs_idata, 'bayes_lasso': lasso_idata})
display(compare)

leaderboard = pd.DataFrame({
    'model':         ['xgboost', 'bayes_lasso', 'horseshoe'],
    'rmse_mph':      [xgb_rmse.mean(), insample_rmse(lasso_idata), insample_rmse(hs_idata)],
    'rmse_type':     ['5x5 CV (out-of-sample)', 'in-sample', 'in-sample'],
}).set_index('model')

In [ ]:






def aggregate_to_pitcher(df, lo, hi, feature_cols):
    """Collapse pitch-level rows to one row per pitcher, using TRAINING winsor bounds."""
    need = set(feature_cols) | {'pitcher_id', 'pitcher_handedness',
                                'player_height', 'hip_shoulder_separation_max'}
    missing = need - set(df.columns)
    assert not missing, f'fcl_df is missing columns: {sorted(missing)}'
    dfc = df.copy()
    dfc[feature_cols] = dfc[feature_cols].clip(lower=lo, upper=hi, axis=1)
    g = dfc.groupby('pitcher_id')
    out = pd.DataFrame({
        'handedness': g['pitcher_handedness'].agg(lambda s: s.mode().iat[0]),
        'height':     g['player_height'].median(),
        'n_pitches':  g.size(),
        'hss_max':    g['hip_shoulder_separation_max'].max(),
    })
    out = out.join(g[feature_cols].mean())
    if 'velocity' in df.columns:                       # current velo, for the gap lens
        out['velo_p95_current'] = g['velocity'].quantile(0.95)
    return out

fcl_agg = aggregate_to_pitcher(fcl_df, lo, hi, feature_cols)

X_fcl = fcl_agg[model_features].to_numpy(dtype=float)
X_fcl = np.where(np.isnan(X_fcl), X_mean, X_fcl)        # impute all-NA feature w/ train mean
X_fcl_std = (X_fcl - X_mean) / X_sd                     # TRAIN-derived standardization

print(f'{X_fcl_std.shape[0]} FCL pitchers, {X_fcl_std.shape[1]} predictors')

























71 FCL pitchers, 64 predictors

























Point + interval predictions (Bayes LASSO)¶
Point = posterior-mean of the regression line. Intervals are 90% posterior predictive (they include the pitcher-level residual sigma, so they answer "what velocity would we expect to see," not just "where is the mean").


















In [ ]:






def bayes_lasso_predict(idata, X_new_std, y_mean, y_sd, ci=0.90, seed=0):
    post = idata.posterior
    beta = post['beta'].stack(s=('chain', 'draw')).values       # (p, S)
    b0   = post['intercept'].stack(s=('chain', 'draw')).values  # (S,)
    sig  = post['sigma'].stack(s=('chain', 'draw')).values      # (S,)
    mu  = b0[None, :] + X_new_std @ beta                        # (n, S), standardized
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    ppc = mu + rng.normal(0, 1, mu.shape) * sig[None, :]        # add observation noise
    to_mph = lambda a: a * y_sd + y_mean
    lo_q, hi_q = (1 - ci) / 2 * 100, (1 + ci) / 2 * 100
    return pd.DataFrame({
        'pred_velo': to_mph(mu.mean(axis=1)),
        'pi_low':    np.percentile(to_mph(ppc), lo_q, axis=1),
        'pi_high':   np.percentile(to_mph(ppc), hi_q, axis=1),
    })

pred = bayes_lasso_predict(lasso_idata, X_fcl_std, y_mean, y_sd, ci=0.90)
pred.index = fcl_agg.index

results = fcl_agg[['handedness', 'n_pitches']].join(pred)
if 'velo_p95_current' in fcl_agg.columns:
    results['velo_p95_current'] = fcl_agg['velo_p95_current']
    results['gap'] = results['pred_velo'] - results['velo_p95_current']
results = results.sort_values('pred_velo', ascending=False)

print(f'Predictions for all {len(results)} FCL pitchers '
      f'(90% posterior-predictive intervals):')
display(results.round(2))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
ax.errorbar(show['pred_velo'], ypos, xerr=err, fmt='none', ecolor='gray', capsize=3)
ax.scatter(show['pred_velo'], ypos, c=colors, zorder=3)
ax.set_yticks(ypos)
ax.set_yticklabels([f'pitcher {i}' for i in show.index])
ax.axhline(len(top5) - 0.5, color='k', lw=0.6, ls='--')
ax.set_xlabel('Projected peak velocity (mph) ± 90% predictive interval')
ax.set_title('FCL pitchers: top 5 (blue) vs bottom 5 (red) by mechanics-implied velocity')
ax.grid(alpha=0.3, axis='x')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

FCL biomechanics percentiles¶
To interpret why the model favors a given arm, it helps to see where each FCL pitcher sits relative to the rest of the FCL field on every biomechanics input. Below:


    

  1. a full percentile table — each FCL pitcher's within-FCL percentile (0–100) for every modeled biomechanics column, and
    2. 

  2. the percentile profile of the pitcher the Bayesian LASSO projects to throw the hardest in five years, sorted from strongest to weakest, with a bar chart highlighting which mechanics are above (blue) or below (red) the FCL median.
    3. 



Percentiles are computed within the 71-pitcher FCL pool on the same winsorized per-pitcher features the model consumes, so a value of 90 means "higher than ~90% of FCL pitchers on this metric."


















In [ ]:






# Percentile rank (0-100) of every FCL pitcher within the FCL pool,
# for each modeled biomechanics column (winsorized means + height + hss_max).
biomech_cols = model_features
fcl_pctile = (fcl_agg[biomech_cols].rank(pct=True) * 100).round(1)
fcl_pctile.index.name = 'pitcher_id'

print(f'Within-FCL biomechanics percentiles: '
      f'{fcl_pctile.shape[0]} pitchers × {fcl_pctile.shape[1]} columns')
display(fcl_pctile)

In [ ]:






# Pitcher the Bayesian LASSO projects to throw hardest (results is sorted desc by pred_velo)
hardest_id = results.index[0]
print(f'Hardest projected FCL pitcher: {hardest_id}  '
      f'(projected {results.loc[hardest_id, "pred_velo"]:.2f} mph, '
      f'{results.loc[hardest_id, "handedness"].upper()}HP)')

hardest_profile = pd.DataFrame({
    'value':             fcl_agg.loc[hardest_id, biomech_cols].round(2),
    'percentile_in_fcl': fcl_pctile.loc[hardest_id],
}).sort_values('percentile_in_fcl', ascending=False)

print(f'\nWithin-FCL percentile profile for pitcher {hardest_id} '
      f'(median percentile = {hardest_profile["percentile_in_fcl"].median():.0f}):')
display(hardest_profile)

# Where are this pitcher's strengths (blue, >=50th pct) and weaknesses (red, <50th)?
order  = hardest_profile.sort_values('percentile_in_fcl')
colors = ['#2c6fbb' if v >= 50 else '#c0392b' for v in order['percentile_in_fcl']]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 14))
ax.barh(order.index, order['percentile_in_fcl'], color=colors)
ax.axvline(50, color='k', lw=0.8, ls='--', label='FCL median')
ax.set(xlabel='Percentile within FCL', xlim=(0, 100),
       title=f'Pitcher {hardest_id}: biomechanics percentiles vs FCL field')
ax.legend(loc='lower right')
ax.grid(alpha=0.3, axis='x')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
